title: Effluent treatment basics
ends: The ETP in-charge wants you on the team.

steps.q: For the same effluent, which is usually higher: COD or BOD?
steps.title: COD vs BOD
steps.summary: COD uses a strong chemical oxidant to oxidise nearly all organic matter and gives a result within hours. BOD measures the oxygen bacteria consume over a few days (3 days at 27 °C in Indian standards), covering only the readily biodegradable part, so COD is almost always higher. Plants track COD daily; BOD shows how well biological treatment can cope.

steps.q: An effluent stream has a BOD/COD ratio of 0.15. What does that tell you?
steps.title: Biodegradability
steps.summary: The BOD/COD ratio indicates how much of the organic load bacteria can degrade. About 0.4 or more treats well biologically; 0.15 means most of the load is hard for bacteria, often due to solvents, toxic or ring compounds, or salt. Segregate such streams and pre-treat them, by solvent recovery, stripping or oxidation, before biological treatment.

draw: BOD ÷ COD = how much is edible

steps.q: 50 m³/day of effluent at 20,000 mg/L COD. What is the daily COD load?
steps.title: COD load
steps.summary: 1 mg/L equals 1 g/m³, so 20,000 mg/L × 50 m³/day = 1,000,000 g/day, or 1000 kg COD per day. The load, not the concentration, sizes biological treatment and aeration, and a small, very strong stream can carry more load than a large dilute one.

steps.q: 1 kg of methanol is lost to drain. Roughly how much COD does it add?
steps.title: Solvent to COD
steps.summary: COD is the oxygen needed to oxidise organics fully. CH₃OH + 1.5 O₂ → CO₂ + 2 H₂O, so 32 g of methanol needs 48 g of oxygen and 1 kg of methanol adds about 1.5 kg of COD. Toluene adds about 3.1 kg COD per kg. Recovering solvent at source is the cheapest COD reduction.

draw: COD = oxygen to burn it all

steps.q: What dissolved oxygen level is usually kept in an aeration tank?
steps.title: Aeration
steps.summary: Aerobic bacteria need oxygen to degrade organics. A dissolved oxygen level of about 1.5 to 2 mg/L keeps them working; below about 1 mg/L treatment slows and sludge quality suffers, while much higher levels waste blower power, often the largest power use in the ETP. Measure DO in the tank and control the blowers on it.

steps.q: A stream has very high TDS (dissolved salts). Will the biological plant remove it?
board: A stream has very high TDS
steps.title: Salts and ZLD
steps.summary: Biological treatment removes organics, not dissolved salts, and high salt stresses the bacteria, so strong saline streams are segregated. They go to a multiple effect evaporator (MEE), and the salt is dried, for example in an agitated thin film dryer, while the condensate is treated or polished and reused. This is how zero liquid discharge (ZLD) plants close the loop.

intro.text: Hi, I'm Bubbles. Today: the effluent plant, where every lost kilogram of solvent ends up. Six questions. Ready?

outro-web.text: That's the lesson. Read the ETP basics guide next.

q1.text: Question 1. For the same effluent, which is usually higher: COD or BOD?

q1-r0.text: BOD only counts what bugs can eat in a few days. COD counts more.

q1-r1.text: Yes! COD oxidises nearly everything, BOD only the easy part.

q1-r2.text: They measure different things, so they're rarely equal.

q1-r3.text: Bugs are picky, not thorough. COD catches what they leave.

q1-b0.text: COD uses a strong chemical oxidant to burn nearly all the organic matter. Result in a few hours.

q1-b1.text: BOD measures the oxygen bacteria use over a few days. In India the test is 3 days at 27 degrees. Only what's easily biodegradable counts.

q1-b2.text: So COD is almost always higher than BOD.

q1-b3.text: Plants track COD daily because it's quick. BOD tells you how well the biology can cope.

q2.text: Question 2. An effluent stream has a BOD/COD ratio of 0.15. What does that tell you?

q2-r0.text: Easy would be 0.4 or more. 0.15 is tough going.

q2-r1.text: Yes! The bugs can't eat most of it.

q2-r2.text: It has plenty. The bugs just don't like them.

q2-r3.text: Maybe, but 0.15 is common for pharma effluent.

q2-b0.text: The BOD to COD ratio shows how much of the organic load bacteria can actually eat.

q2-b1.text: Around 0.4 or more treats well biologically. 0.15 means most of it is hard for the bugs.

q2-b2.text: Typical culprits: solvents the bugs dislike, toxic or ring compounds, and high salt.

q2-b3.text: Treat that stream separately first: recover the solvent, strip it, or pre-treat it, before it reaches the aeration tank.

q3.text: Question 3. 50 m³/day of effluent at 20,000 mg/L COD. What is the daily COD load?

q3-r0.text: Ten times too little. Milligrams per litre is grams per cubic metre.

q3-r2.text: Ten times too much. Check the units.

q3-r3.text: That's the concentration, not the load.

q3-b0.text: Milligrams per litre is the same as grams per cubic metre.

q3-b1.text: 20,000 grams per cubic metre times 50 cubic metres is a million grams. 1000 kilograms a day.

q3-b2.text: Load, not concentration, sizes the biology and the aeration.

q3-b3.text: A small stream at very high COD can carry more load than a big dilute one. Find those streams first.

q4.text: Question 4. 1 kg of methanol is lost to drain. Roughly how much COD does it add?

q4-r0.text: Too little. Burning it takes more oxygen than its own weight.

q4-r2.text: Close, but oxidising methanol takes 1.5 times its weight in oxygen.

q4-r3.text: Some evaporates, but plenty stays in the water.

q4-b0.text: COD is the oxygen needed to oxidise the organics fully.

q4-b1.text: Methanol plus one and a half oxygen molecules gives carbon dioxide and water.

q4-b2.text: 32 grams of methanol needs 48 grams of oxygen. So 1 kilogram adds about 1.5 kilograms of COD.

q4-b3.text: Toluene is worse, about 3.1 kilograms of COD per kilogram. Recovering solvent is the cheapest COD reduction there is.

q5.text: Question 5. What dissolved oxygen level is usually kept in an aeration tank?

q5-r0.text: Zero oxygen and the aerobic bugs suffocate.

q5-r2.text: Near saturation wastes blower power for little gain.

q5-r3.text: Higher just costs power. The bugs are happy at about 2.

q5-b0.text: Aerobic bacteria need oxygen to eat the organics. Blowers or surface aerators supply it.

q5-b1.text: About 1.5 to 2 milligrams per litre keeps them working. Below 1, they slow down and the sludge can turn bad.

q5-b2.text: Much higher just burns blower power. Aeration is often the biggest power user in the ETP.

q5-b3.text: Measure dissolved oxygen in the tank, and control the blowers on it.

q6.text: Question 6. A stream has very high TDS (dissolved salts). Will the biological plant remove it?

q6-r0.text: Bugs don't eat salt. Too much of it actually harms them.

q6-r1.text: Correct! Biology removes organics, not salts.

q6-r2.text: More air won't make salt disappear.

q6-r3.text: More sludge won't take the salt out of the water.

q6-b0.text: Biological treatment removes organics. Dissolved salts pass straight through.

q6-b1.text: High salt also stresses the bacteria, so strong salty streams are kept apart.

q6-b2.text: Salty streams go to a multiple effect evaporator, the MEE. The salt is then dried, for example in an agitated thin film dryer.

q6-b3.text: The condensate goes back through treatment or polishing, then gets reused. That's how zero liquid discharge, ZLD, plants close the loop. More in the ETP basics guide on pharmacheme dot in.
